questions.q: What single underlying idea connects every concept in this chapter?
options: How to configure Fabric Capacity SKUs
How to design a Power BI semantic model
How to compute correct, timely answers over data that never stops arriving
How to write T-SQL stored procedures
questions.explain: Chapter 1 was storage and structure sitting still; Chapter 2 was data in motion, and every concept exists because motion breaks batch assumptions.

questions.q: What are the two real ingestion paths into a KQL Database covered in this chapter?
options: Only Fabric Data Factory Copy activity
Only streaming — batch ingestion isn't possible with KQL Databases
Only Power BI Direct Lake refresh
Streaming via Eventstream, and batch via .ingest into table
questions.explain: Lesson 27 covered both: continuous Eventstream destinations for live data, and one-time batch loads for existing files.

questions.q: What are the three window shapes covered, and what distinguishes them?
options: Tumbling (fixed, no overlap), hopping/sliding (fixed, overlapping), and session (variable, closed by a gap)
Small, medium, and large windows, distinguished only by size
Batch, streaming, and hybrid windows
KQL windows, Power BI windows, and Databricks windows
questions.explain: Each answers a different question: "every N minutes," "a smooth rolling view," or "how long was this burst of activity."

questions.q: According to the chapter's throughline, why do windows, watermarks, and out-of-order handling all exist?
options: They were all invented independently with no shared root cause
They only exist because of a specific limitation in KQL syntax
They all trace back to the fact that a stream has no natural stopping point — windows need a boundary, watermarks need a closing rule, and network reality doesn't respect event order
They exist purely for cost optimization, with no connection to the nature of streaming itself
questions.explain: None of this chapter's complexity is arbitrary — it's what "always on" actually requires.

questions.q: What does Chapter 3 (Production Data Engineering) shift the focus toward?
options: Returning to batch-only processing with no real-time component
Building a completely new set of Fabric items unrelated to Chapters 1-2
Replacing KQL entirely with a different query language
Running pipelines reliably at scale — CI/CD, testing, observability, cost management, incident response, and governance
questions.explain: Chapter 3 shifts from building correct pipelines to operating them reliably for everything built across all three courses in this track.
